explanation: Das regelmäßige Simple Past bildet man mit Grundform + -ed. Schreibweise: Nach kurzem, betontem Vokal wird der Endkonsonant verdoppelt (stop → stopped), ein stummes -e fällt weg (like → liked), -y nach Konsonant wird zu -ied (study → studied). Die Form ist bei allen Personen gleich. Die -ing-Form (walking) ist die Verlaufsform, nicht die Vergangenheit; der Vokalwechsel (sing → sang) kommt nur bei unregelmäßigen Verben vor.
options: Add -ed to the base form: walk → walked, play → played
Add -s to the base form: walk → walks, play → plays, want → wants
Add -ing to the base form: walk → walking, play → playing, want → wanting
Change the stem vowel: sing → sang, drink → drank
question: How is the Simple Past of regular verbs formed?

explanation: Die Verneinung lautet: Subjekt + did not (didn't) + Grundform. "She didn't come." – NICHT "She didn't came." Did ist das Hilfsverb und trägt schon die Vergangenheit, deshalb bleibt das Hauptverb in der Grundform. Ausnahme ist be: was not / were not, ganz ohne did. "Have not + Partizip" wäre das Present Perfect, "was not + -ing" das Past Progressive.
options: Put not after the main verb: She went not to school. He knew not the answer.
Use did not (didn't) + base form: She didn't go.
Use have not (haven't) + past participle: She hasn't gone. He hasn't known.
Use was/were not + verb-ing: She wasn't going. He wasn't knowing.
question: How do you form the negative in Simple Past?

explanation: Fragen im Simple Past bildet man mit Did + Subjekt + Grundform: "Did he call?" – NICHT "Did he called?" und NICHT "Do he called?" Weil did schon die Vergangenheit anzeigt, bleibt das Hauptverb in der Grundform. Ausnahme ist be: Was/Were + Subjekt, z. B. "Was she there?" Kurzantworten: Yes, she did. / No, she didn't.
options: Main verb first + subject: Went she? Saw you it?
Was/were + subject + verb-ing: Was she going? Were you seeing it?
Did + subject + base form: Did she go? Did you see it?
Do + subject + past form: Do she went? Do you saw it?
question: How do you form questions in Simple Past?

explanation: Unregelmäßige Verben muss man auswendig lernen: go → went, come → came, see → saw, say → said, get → got, make → made, know → knew, think → thought, take → took, give → gave. "Gone" ist das Partizip (die 3. Form, z. B. in I have gone), "goes" die Präsensform der 3. Person Einzahl.
options: Goed
Goes
Gone
Went
question: What is the Simple Past of "go"?

explanation: Das Simple Past beschreibt eine abgeschlossene Handlung zu einem genannten Zeitpunkt in der Vergangenheit: "I visited Paris last year." Signalwörter (typische Begleitwörter) sind: yesterday, last night/week/year, in 2020, two days ago, when I was young. Zum Vergleich: Beim Present Perfect wird kein bestimmter Zeitpunkt genannt.
options: For finished actions at a stated past time, with signal words like yesterday, ago, in 2020
For repeated habits in the present, with signal words like always, often, every day
For actions in progress in the past, with signal words like while, as, at that moment
For plans and intentions in the future, with signal words like tomorrow, next week, soon
question: When do we use the Simple Past?

explanation: "To be" hat im Simple Past zwei Formen: was bei I, he, she, it – were bei you, we, they. "I was happy." "They were late." Fragen bildet man ohne did, einfach durch Umstellung: "Was he there?" "Were you ready?" Verneinung: wasn't / weren't.
options: Was for all persons: I was, you was, he was, we was, they was
Was for I/he/she/it and were for you/we/they: I was, they were
Were for all persons: I were, you were, he were, we were, they were
Was for the plural and were for the singular: I were, he were, we was
question: What are the forms of "to be" in Simple Past?

explanation: Das Past Progressive ist die Verlaufsform der Vergangenheit: was/were + -ing. Es zeigt, dass eine Handlung zu einem bestimmten Zeitpunkt gerade lief: "I was sleeping at 10 pm." Oft wird sie unterbrochen: "While I was cooking, she called." Unterschied: Simple Past = kurze, abgeschlossene Handlung, Past Progressive = längere Handlung im Hintergrund. Am/is/are + -ing ist dagegen das Present Progressive, also die Gegenwart.
options: A short, completed action in the past, formed with the past form of the verb
An action planned for a later time, formed with will + be + verb-ing
An action in progress at a moment in the past: was/were + verb-ing
An action happening at this very moment, formed with am/is/are + verb-ing
question: What is the Past Progressive (Past Continuous)?

explanation: Das Present Perfect bildet man mit have/has + Partizip Perfekt (der 3. Verbform): "I have eaten." "She has visited." Das Partizip ist bei regelmäßigen Verben die -ed-Form, bei unregelmäßigen muss man es lernen (go → gone, see → seen, eat → eaten). Ein bestimmter Zeitpunkt wird dabei nicht genannt. "Did" steht nie zusammen mit einem Partizip.
options: did + past participle: I did seen, she did gone
was/were + verb-ing: I was seeing, she was going, we were finishing
will + base form: I will see, she will go
have/has + past participle: I have seen, she has gone
question: How is the Present Perfect formed?

explanation: Simple Past: "I saw her yesterday." – der Zeitpunkt wird genannt, die Sache ist abgeschlossen. Present Perfect: "I have seen her before." – kein bestimmter Zeitpunkt, es geht um Erfahrung oder um die Bedeutung für jetzt. Signalwörter: Simple Past mit yesterday, last year, ago, in 2010; Present Perfect mit ever, never, already, just, yet, since, for.
options: Simple Past: finished action at a stated time. Present Perfect: relevance now or no stated time
Simple Past is used in writing, Present Perfect is used only in spoken language
Simple Past: relevance for now. Present Perfect: a finished action at a clearly stated time
Simple Past is used with irregular verbs, Present Perfect only with regular verbs
question: What is the difference between Simple Past and Present Perfect?

explanation: Kurze Adjektive (ein bis zwei Silben) werden mit -er/-est gesteigert: tall → taller → tallest. Schreibweise: Konsonant verdoppeln (big → bigger), -y wird zu -ier (happy → happier). Lange Adjektive nehmen more/most: useful → more useful → the most useful. Unregelmäßig: good → better → best, bad → worse → worst, far → further → furthest. Nie beides gleichzeitig – "more bigger" ist falsch.
options: Add -er/-est to every adjective: beautiful → beautifuler, big → bigger, good → gooder
Add -er/-est to short adjectives and more/most to long ones: bigger, the most useful
Add more/most to every adjective: more big → most big, more beautiful → most beautiful
Add more/most to short adjectives and -er/-est to long ones: more big, beautifuler
question: What are comparative and superlative forms of adjectives?

explanation: Der If-Satz Typ 1 beschreibt eine mögliche, realistische Bedingung: "If I study hard, I will pass the exam." Im if-Satz (dem Bedingungssatz) steht Simple Present – niemals will! Im Hauptsatz steht will + Grundform. Statt will können auch andere Modalverben stehen: "If it rains, we can/might/should stay inside."
options: An unreal condition now: If + Simple Past, would + base form (If I had time, I would come)
An impossible past condition: If + Past Perfect, would have + participle (If I had known)
A real or possible condition: If + Simple Present, will + base form
A general truth: If + Simple Present, Simple Present (If you heat water, it boils)
question: What is an if-clause type 1?

explanation: Much steht bei nicht zählbaren Dingen, die man nicht einzeln zählen kann: much money, much information, much homework. Many steht bei zählbaren Dingen in der Mehrzahl: many cars, many students, many ideas. In bejahten Sätzen benutzt man meist a lot of – das passt zu beidem. Much und many stehen vor allem in Verneinungen und Fragen, aber nicht nur dort.
options: Much with countable nouns (much books, much cars), many with uncountable nouns (many water)
Much with plural nouns (much cars), many with singular nouns (many idea)
Much in questions only (How much?), many in statements only (I have many)
Much with uncountable nouns (much water), many with countable nouns (many books)
question: What is the difference between "much" and "many"?

explanation: "Used to" beschreibt eine Gewohnheit oder einen Zustand, der früher galt und heute nicht mehr: "I used to play football." – früher ja, heute nicht mehr. Frage: "Did you use to ...?" Verneinung: "I didn't use to ..." (dort ohne -d). Für ein einmaliges Ereignis passt es nicht: "I broke my arm last summer" – nicht "used to break".
options: A habit or state in the past that is over: I used to live in Berlin, but not anymore
A habit that is still true today: I used to live in Berlin and I still live there
An intention for the future: I used to move to Berlin at the end of next year
A single event at one moment in the past: I used to break my arm last summer
question: What does "used to" express?

explanation: Modalverben sind Hilfsverben, die Fähigkeit, Erlaubnis oder Verpflichtung ausdrücken. Nach ihnen steht immer die Grundform des Hauptverbs – ohne -s, ohne -ed und ohne to. Can (Fähigkeit oder Erlaubnis): I can swim. Must (Pflicht): You must stop. Should (Rat): You should eat well. May/might (Möglichkeit). Could (Fähigkeit in der Vergangenheit oder höfliche Bitte).
options: Verbs that name a concrete action: run, eat, write, build, speak, work, play
Auxiliary verbs for ability, permission or obligation: can, must, should
Verbs with irregular past forms: go/went, see/saw, take/took, know/knew, give/gave
Verbs that link subject and complement: be, seem, become, look
question: What are modal verbs in English?

explanation: Can steht für eine Fähigkeit oder Erlaubnis in der Gegenwart: "I can speak German." Could steht für eine Fähigkeit in der Vergangenheit ("I could run fast as a child"), für eine höfliche Bitte ("Could you open the door?") oder für eine Möglichkeit ("It could rain."). Could klingt vorsichtiger und höflicher als can.
options: Both express present ability in exactly the same way and can always be swapped
Can: ability in the past. Could: ability and permission in the present moment
Can: ability or permission now. Could: past ability or polite request
Can: used in questions only. Could: used in statements and short answers only
question: What is the difference between "can" and "could"?

explanation: Das Passiv (die Leideform) bildet man mit be + Partizip Perfekt. Aktiv: "They built the bridge." Passiv: "The bridge was built (by them)." Das Objekt des Aktivsatzes wird also zum Subjekt, und wer es getan hat, kann wegfallen. In den Zeiten: is written (Gegenwart), was written (Vergangenheit), has been written (Present Perfect), will be written (Zukunft).
options: The subject does the action itself: She wrote the book, formed with the past form
The action is shown as ongoing: She was writing the book, formed with be + verb-ing
The action is put into the perfect: She has written the book, formed with have + participle
The object becomes the subject: The book was written by her, formed with be + participle
question: What is the passive voice in English?

explanation: Relativsätze beschreiben ein Nomen genauer. Sie beginnen mit einem Relativpronomen: who für Personen, which für Sachen, that für beides (eher umgangssprachlich). "The book that/which I read was great." "The woman who/that called is my teacher." Whose zeigt Besitz an: "The student whose bag I found ..."
options: Clauses that describe a noun with who, which or that: The man who lives there is my uncle.
Clauses that stand alone as full sentences: The man lives there. He is my uncle.
Clauses that state a condition with if: If the man lives there, he is my uncle.
Clauses that give a reason with because or so: He is my uncle because he lives there.
question: What are relative clauses in English?

explanation: Das Gerundium ist die -ing-Form, die wie ein Nomen benutzt wird. Als Subjekt: "Swimming is healthy." Nach bestimmten Verben wie enjoy, avoid, mind, finish, suggest, keep: "I enjoy swimming." Und immer nach Präpositionen (kleinen Verhältniswörtern wie at, of, about): "I'm good at cooking."
options: The -ing form after be, showing an action in progress: She is swimming at the moment.
The -ing form used as a noun, as subject or object: Swimming is fun. I enjoy reading.
The base form with to, used after want or hope: I want to swim. I hope to read a lot.
The third form of the verb, used after have or be: I have swum. The book was read.
question: What is the gerund in English?

explanation: Der Infinitiv mit to steht nach Verben wie want, decide, hope: want to go, decide to stay, hope to win. Außerdem gibt er einen Zweck an: "I study to learn." – um zu lernen. Auch nach bestimmten Adjektiven: "glad to help." Nach Modalverben steht kein to (can do, must go); nach Präpositionen und nach enjoy/avoid/finish steht das Gerundium (die -ing-Form), nicht der Infinitiv.
options: After modal verbs such as can, must and should: I can to swim, she must to go
After prepositions such as at, of and about: I am good at to cook, afraid of to fall
After verbs like want or decide and to express a purpose: I went there to buy milk
After verbs like enjoy, avoid and finish: I enjoy to swim, she avoids to run in the rain
question: What is the infinitive with "to" used for?

explanation: Since nennt den Startpunkt, seit dem etwas gilt: "I have lived here since 2015." For nennt die Dauer, also wie lange: "I have lived here for 8 years." Nach since steht ein Zeitpunkt: Monday, January, 2010, I was a child. Nach for steht ein Zeitraum: two hours, a long time, ages, three weeks.
options: Both name the length of a period of time and can be used in exactly the same way
Since names the duration (since three years), for names the starting point (for Monday)
Since is used with countable periods, for is used with uncountable periods of time
Since names the starting point, for names the duration
question: What does "since" vs "for" express with Present Perfect?

explanation: Diese unregelmäßigen Verben sollte man sicher können, jeweils in den drei Formen Grundform / Simple Past / Partizip: be/was-were/been, have/had/had, do/did/done, go/went/gone, come/came/come, see/saw/seen, give/gave/given, take/took/taken, write/wrote/written, speak/spoke/spoken.
options: go/went/gone, see/saw/seen, do/did/done, have/had/had, take/took/taken
goed, comed, seed, doed, haved, sayed, getted, maked, knowed, taked
be/was/been is the single irregular verb; all other verbs follow the -ed pattern
walk/walked/walked, play/played/played, want/wanted/wanted
question: What are the most common irregular verbs students should know?

explanation: In der indirekten Rede gibt man wieder, was jemand gesagt hat, ohne die genauen Worte zu wiederholen: "I am tired" → She said (that) she was tired. Dabei rückt die Zeitform eine Stufe zurück: Gegenwart → Vergangenheit, Vergangenheit → Past Perfect, will → would. Auch die Pronomen ändern sich, ebenso Zeit- und Ortsangaben (here → there, now → then, today → that day).
options: Repeating the exact words of a speaker in quotation marks: She said, "I am tired."
Telling what someone said without the exact words: She said (that) she was tired.
Turning a statement into a question about the words used: What did she say to you?
Writing a dialogue with a new line for every speaker: – I am tired. – Me too.
question: What is reported speech (indirect speech)?

explanation: Häufigkeitsadverbien sagen, wie oft etwas passiert: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, seldom, never. Stellung im Satz: vor dem Hauptverb ("I always eat breakfast"), aber nach Formen von "be" ("She is always late"). Weitere Beispiele: "Do you ever ...?" "I have never been ..."
options: A word that describes a noun more closely: a red car, an old house, three books
A word that makes an adjective stronger or weaker: very good, quite old, rather cold
A word that tells how often something happens: always, usually, often, sometimes, never
A word that says where or when an action happens: here, outside, yesterday, soon
question: What is an adverb of frequency?

explanation: Fragen mit Fragewort haben die Reihenfolge: Fragewort (Who, What, Where, When, Why, How) + Hilfsverb + Subjekt + Verb. "Where did you go?" – nach did steht die Grundform. "What have you eaten?" – nach have steht das Partizip. Ausnahme: Fragt who oder what nach dem Subjekt, braucht man kein Hilfsverb: "Who called?"
options: Question word + subject + main verb: Where you went? What you have eaten?
Question word + main verb + subject: Where went you? What ate you yesterday?
Subject + verb with the question word at the end: You went where? She is crying why?
Question word + auxiliary + subject + main verb: Where did you go?
question: What is the structure of a question with a question word?

explanation: Das Present Perfect verbindet Vergangenheit und Gegenwart. Bedeutung für jetzt: "I have lost my key." – der Schlüssel ist immer noch weg. Simple Past dagegen: "I lost my key yesterday." – eine abgeschlossene Tatsache. Erfahrung: "Have you ever been to Italy?" Gerade abgeschlossen: "She has just finished." Noch nicht abgeschlossener Zeitraum: "I have lived here for 5 years."
options: It links the past to the present: experience, recent action, unfinished period
It is simply the more formal version of the Simple Past, used mainly in written texts
It is the more polite form, used for requests in spoken conversation
It describes actions further back in the past than the Simple Past
question: What does the Present Perfect express that is different from Simple Past?

explanation: A und an sind die unbestimmten Artikel. A steht vor einem Konsonantenlaut: a book, a university (klingt wie "juniversity"), a European. An steht vor einem Vokallaut: an apple, an elephant, an hour (das h ist stumm), an honest man. Entscheidend ist also der Laut, nicht der geschriebene Buchstabe.
options: A stands before countable nouns (a car), an before uncountable nouns (an water)
A stands before consonant sounds (a car, a university), an before vowel sounds (an hour)
A stands before singular nouns (a car), an before plural nouns (an cars, an apples)
A stands before short words (a car), an before longer words (an bicycle, an teacher)
question: What is the difference between "a" and "an"?

explanation: Präpositionen sind kleine Verhältniswörter. Bei Zeitangaben gilt: at bei genauen Uhrzeiten (at 3 pm, at midnight, at Christmas), on bei einzelnen Tagen und Daten (on Monday, on my birthday, on 5th June), in bei längeren Zeiträumen (in the morning, in July, in 2020, in winter).
options: At for days and dates, on for exact times, in for months: at Monday, on 5pm, in July
In for exact times, at for months and years, on for seasons: in 5pm, at July, on summer
At for exact times (at 5pm), on for days (on Monday), in for months (in July)
At for every time expression: at 5pm, at Monday, at July, at 2020
question: What are prepositions of time in English?

explanation: Bei Ortsangaben gilt: in bei einem umschlossenen Raum (in the room, in the box), on bei einer Oberfläche (on the shelf, on the table), at bei einem Punkt oder Treffpunkt (at home, at the door, at the bus stop). Weitere Ortspräpositionen: under/below, over/above, next to, beside, between (zwischen zwei Dingen), among (unter vielen).
options: In for surfaces, on for closed spaces, at for larger areas: in the table, on the box
On for closed spaces, at for surfaces, in for exact points: on the box, at the table, in the door
At for every place expression: at the box, at the table, at the door, at the shelf
In for closed spaces (in the box), on for surfaces (on the table)
question: What are prepositions of place in English?

explanation: Make benutzt man, wenn etwas Neues entsteht: make a phone call, make dinner, make friends, make a plan, make a decision. Do benutzt man für Tätigkeiten, bei denen nichts Greifbares hergestellt wird: do sport, do homework, do business, do a favour, do your best. Vieles davon sind feste Wendungen, die man einfach lernen muss.
options: Make for creating something (make a cake), do for activities (do homework, sport)
Both verbs mean the same and can be used in every fixed expression alike
Make for activities (make homework, make sport), do for creating something (do a cake)
Make is used in questions and do in statements, with the same meaning
question: What is the difference between "make" and "do" in English?

explanation: "There is / there are" sagt, dass etwas vorhanden ist – auf Deutsch "es gibt". There is + Einzahl: "There is a problem." There are + Mehrzahl: "There are many people." Vergangenheit: There was / There were. Frage: Is there ...? Are there ...? Verneinung: There isn't / There aren't. Nicht mit "they are" verwechseln.
options: Another way of saying "it is", with exactly the same meaning: There is cold today.
A way of saying that something exists: there is + singular, there are + plural nouns
A short form of "they are": There are happy today. There are going home now.
A phrase that always takes the plural form: There are a problem. There are one cat.
question: What is "there is / there are"?

explanation: Zeitliche Verknüpfungswörter ordnen Handlungen in eine Reihenfolge: First → Then → After that → Finally. Dazu kommen: when (wenn/als), while (während, gleichzeitig), before und after (vorher und nachher), as soon as (sobald), until (bis zu einem Zeitpunkt), during (während eines ganzen Zeitraums).
options: And, but, or, as well as – they add information or set two ideas against each other
Because, so, therefore, although, however – they give reasons, results or contrast
First, then, after that, finally, when, while, before, after, as soon as, until
Who, which, that, whose – they attach a description to a noun in the sentence
question: What are the most important time connectors in English?

explanation: Meist hängt man -ing einfach an: walk → walking, play → playing. Nach einem kurzen, betonten Vokal mit nur einem Endkonsonanten wird dieser verdoppelt: sit → sitting, stop → stopping. Ein stummes -e am Ende fällt weg: make → making, write → writing. Ein -ie wird zu -y: lie → lying, die → dying.
options: Add -ing to the base form unchanged: ride → rideing, swim → swiming, lie → lieing
Double the final consonant in every verb: walk → walkking, ride → ridding, play → playying
Change every final -y to -ie before -ing: play → plaieing, study → studieing, try → trieing
Double the consonant after a short vowel (swim → swimming), drop silent -e (ride → riding)
question: What is the rule for spelling -ing forms?

explanation: Falsche Freunde sind Wörter, die in beiden Sprachen ähnlich aussehen, aber etwas anderes bedeuten: gift heißt Geschenk (deutsch Gift = poison), become heißt werden (deutsch bekommen = receive), sympathetic heißt mitfühlend (deutsch sympathisch = likeable), art heißt Kunst (deutsch Art = type), chef heißt Küchenchef (deutsch Chef = boss).
options: Words that look alike but mean different things: become vs. bekommen
Words of both languages that rhyme with each other: house/Haus, mouse/Maus, garden/Garten
Words that English has taken from German unchanged: kindergarten, rucksack, hamburger
Words with the same meaning inside one language: big and large, start and begin
question: What are "false friends" between German and English?

explanation: Der Imperativ ist die Befehlsform: die Grundform des Verbs, ganz ohne Subjekt. "Open the window." Verneint mit don't: "Don't run." Höflicher wird es mit please ("Please be quiet.") oder mit einer Frage ("Could you ...?"). Das Subjekt (you) ist mitgemeint, deshalb steht es nicht da. Zur Verstärkung kann do davorstehen: "Do sit down!"
options: The question form of the verb: Do you go? Are you listening carefully to me?
The base form used for orders and requests: Go! Listen carefully! Please sit down.
The past form used to report an order: He went. She listened carefully to the teacher.
Subject + will used for promises: You will go. You will listen carefully to me.
question: What is the imperative in English?

explanation: Britisches und amerikanisches Englisch unterscheiden sich in mehreren Bereichen. Schreibung: -our/-or (colour/color), -re/-er (centre/center), -ise/-ize. Wortschatz: lorry/truck, lift/elevator, biscuit/cookie, chemist/drugstore, post/mail. Auch die Aussprache ist anders. Dazu kommen kleine Unterschiede in der Grammatik: Bei gerade Geschehenem steht im britischen Englisch eher das Present Perfect, im amerikanischen oft das Simple Past. Beide Varianten sind richtig.
options: The spelling differs (colour/color), while vocabulary, grammar and sound are identical
The pronunciation differs, while spelling, vocabulary and grammar follow the same rules
Spelling, vocabulary, pronunciation and some grammar differ: colour/color, lift/elevator
The vocabulary differs (lift/elevator), while spelling and pronunciation stay the same
question: What are the main differences between British and American English?

explanation: Diese Wortpaare gehören immer zusammen und verbinden zwei Teile: both A and B heißt sowohl A als auch B – beide sind gemeint. Either A or B heißt entweder A oder B – eines von beiden. Neither A nor B heißt weder A noch B – keines von beiden. Beispiele: "Both cats and dogs are popular pets." "Either you study or you fail." "Neither she nor I knew."
options: Both...and excludes two things, either...or includes both, neither...nor offers a choice
All three connect events in time, like before, after, as soon as and until in a sentence
All three introduce a condition, like if, unless and provided that in a sentence
Both...and includes two, either...or offers one of two, neither...nor excludes both
question: What does "both ... and", "either ... or", "neither ... nor" express?

explanation: Ein Phrasal Verb besteht aus einem Verb und einem kleinen Zusatzwort (Partikel); zusammen ergeben sie eine neue Bedeutung, die man aus den Einzelteilen oft nicht erraten kann: give up (aufgeben), look after (sich kümmern um), look forward to (sich freuen auf), put off (verschieben), get on with (auskommen mit), run out of (ausgehen), turn off (ausschalten), find out (herausfinden). Sie sind im Englischen sehr häufig und müssen gelernt werden.
options: A verb plus a particle with a new meaning: give up, look after, turn off, find out
A verb with an unusually large number of letters: understand, congratulate, remember
A verb that is followed by an auxiliary: can go, must stay, should wait
A verb that forms its past tense with -ed: walked, played, wanted, lived, worked
question: What is a phrasal verb?

explanation: Nach "say" folgt direkt der Inhalt, ohne dass die angesprochene Person genannt wird: He said (that) he was tired. Nach "tell" muss dagegen die Person stehen, der etwas gesagt wird: He told me (that) he was tired – tell me, tell him, tell the class. Typischer Fehler: "He said me" ist falsch, richtig ist "He told me".
options: Both verbs work alike and can be used with or without a person as object
Say works without naming the listener (She said it was cold), tell needs a person (She told me)
Say needs a person as object (She said me), tell works without a listener (She told it was cold)
Say is used in questions and tell in statements, otherwise the meaning is the same
question: What is the difference between "say" and "tell"?

explanation: See heißt sehen, ohne dass man sich anstrengt – man nimmt etwas einfach wahr (I see a bird, can you see it?). Look (at) heißt, den Blick absichtlich auf etwas richten (look at the map). Watch heißt, etwas Bewegtes über längere Zeit verfolgen (watch the film, watch the children play). Genauso funktioniert das Paar hear und listen to.
options: The three verbs mean the same and can replace each other in every sentence
See: follow something moving. Look at: perceive without effort. Watch: direct the gaze briefly
See: perceive without effort. Look at: direct the gaze on purpose. Watch: follow something moving
See is used for people, look for objects and watch for places, buildings and rooms

explanation: Artikel stehen vor einem Nomen. Den unbestimmten Artikel a/an benutzt man, wenn etwas zum ersten Mal genannt wird: "I saw a dog." Den bestimmten Artikel the benutzt man, wenn die Sache schon bekannt oder einmalig ist: "The dog was huge.", "the sun", "the Queen". Bei allgemeinen Aussagen steht gar kein Artikel: "Dogs are friendly.", "I love music." Besonderheiten: the bei Superlativen und bei Flussnamen ("the Rhine").
options: Short words placed before a noun to show its case: of, to, with, from, by
Short words that stand in for a noun in the sentence: he, she, it, they, them
Short words that describe a noun more closely: big, red, old, beautiful, heavy
A/an introduces something new, the points to something known
